claims.text: Systematically increasing lattice distortion in refractory high-entropy alloys will enhance elastic anisotropy.
Increasing lattice distortion will modify dislocation core energetics.
Increasing lattice distortion will promote edge-dislocation dominance.
The lattice-distortion-induced changes in anisotropy and dislocation behavior will raise high-temperature yield strength.
The baseline material is a single-phase BCC refractory HEA with minimal lattice distortion and controlled impurity levels.
The minimally distorted baseline will exhibit conventional elastic and dislocation behavior at high temperature.
Atomic-size-mismatch variations or minor impurity additions can be used to systematically increase lattice distortion.
Grain size, phase constitution, and processing conditions will be held constant while lattice distortion is varied.
Increased lattice distortion alters local atomic arrangements.
Increased lattice distortion reduces the activation energy for edge-dislocation propagation relative to screw-dislocation propagation.
Preferential edge-dislocation propagation produces a deformation mechanism that increases elevated-temperature yield strength.
The more distorted alloy will show greater elastic-modulus anisotropy than the baseline.
The more distorted alloy will show a shift toward edge-dislocation signatures relative to the baseline.
The more distorted alloy will have a higher yield strength than the baseline under identical high-temperature conditions.
The conventional BCC refractory-HEA baseline is expected to be screw-dislocation dominated at high temperature.
In-situ neutron diffraction can determine temperature-dependent elastic anisotropy and elastic moduli in a BCC refractory HEA.
The proposed effect is limited to temperatures above 800°C.
Nanoscale phase heterogeneities and other microstructural features may obscure the quantitative relationship between lattice distortion, elastic anisotropy, and yield strength.
